topic: The Pathophysiology of Sepsis — From Infection to Dysregulated Host Response
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Department of Intensive Care Medicine
speakerBio: An intensivist-immunologist who has spent two decades studying why the body's defence turns on itself. Insists that nobody should give a drop of fluid or a gram of antibiotic until they can draw the endothelium failing.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

A 68-year-old woman with a UTI is admitted to the ward "for IV antibiotics." Six hours later she is confused, mottled to the knees, tachycardic at 120, and her lactate is 4.2. She has the same bug she walked in with — yet she is dying. Why? Because sepsis is not the infection. Sepsis is what her own body did in response to it. To understand every guideline that follows this week, you must first understand the dysregulated host response.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The infection lights the match; the immune system burns the house down.

This is the Sepsis-3 definition (2016), and every word is load-bearing. Infection alone is not sepsis — millions of people have infections and are fine. Organ dysfunction is what makes it sepsis. And the dysfunction is not primarily caused by the pathogen's toxins — it is caused by the host's own defensive response spiralling out of proportion. The enemy, in a real sense, becomes friendly fire.

2 · The trigger — how the body knows there is an invader 🦠

The innate immune system does not need to have "seen" a specific microbe before. It recognises molecular patterns that are shared across whole classes of danger. Two families of danger signals kick everything off:

SignalWhat it isExamples
PAMPs — pathogen-associated molecular patternsConserved molecular signatures of microbes — the "barcode" of an invaderLipopolysaccharide (LPS/endotoxin) of Gram-negatives, lipoteichoic acid & peptidoglycan of Gram-positives, flagellin, bacterial/viral nucleic acids, fungal β-glucan
DAMPs — damage-associated molecular patternsThe body's own molecules, released by injured/dying cells — the "barcode" of tissue damageMitochondrial DNA, HMGB1, ATP, heat-shock proteins, histones, uric acid

Both bind to pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) on immune and endothelial cells — most famously the Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (e.g. TLR4 for LPS), plus NOD-like receptors and the inflammasome. Engagement of these receptors is the ignition switch: it activates NF-κB, the master transcription factor of inflammation.

💡 One-liner

PAMPs say "there is an invader." DAMPs say "there is damage." Both scream through the same alarm (PRRs → NF-κB) — which is why sterile insults (pancreatitis, burns, trauma) can look exactly like sepsis. Same fire alarm, different smoke.

3 · The pro-inflammatory storm 🔥 — the cytokine cascade

NF-κB activation floods the circulation with pro-inflammatory cytokines. The three you must know cold:

  • TNF-α — the earliest and most powerful. Injecting TNF alone into an animal reproduces the shock state. Drives fever, endothelial activation, and further cytokine release.
  • IL-1β — synergises with TNF, resets the hypothalamic thermostat (fever), amplifies the cascade.
  • IL-6 — the great amplifier and messenger; drives the hepatic acute-phase response (CRP, procalcitonin, fibrinogen). Blood IL-6 levels track severity.

This burst is meant to be local — to contain and kill a pathogen in one tissue. In sepsis it becomes systemic and self-sustaining: cytokines beget more cytokines in a feed-forward loop popularly called the "cytokine storm." Complement (C5a), the coagulation cascade, and the kallikrein–kinin system are all activated in parallel, so inflammation and clotting rise together.

4 · The endothelium — where the disease actually lives 🩸

Here is the conceptual leap that separates people who understand sepsis from people who memorise it: sepsis is fundamentally a disease of the endothelium. The single layer of cells lining every vessel is normally an anticoagulant, barrier-forming, vasoregulating organ. In sepsis it is transformed into a pro-coagulant, leaky, vasodilating liability across the entire body at once.

Two mechanisms do most of the damage:

  1. Glycocalyx shedding. The endothelial glycocalyx is a delicate gel-like sugar coat that keeps the vessel sealed and repels clotting. Inflammatory mediators (TNF, heparanase, MMPs) strip it away. Once shed, the vessel wall becomes leaky and thrombogenic — this is the molecular origin of capillary leak.
  2. Endothelial activation. Activated endothelium up-regulates adhesion molecules (selectins, ICAM/VCAM), expresses tissue factor, and pumps out inducible nitric oxide (via iNOS). Widened intercellular junctions let protein-rich fluid pour into the interstitium.
🎯 Key concept — capillary leak

A shed glycocalyx + opened endothelial junctions = fluid, albumin, and electrolytes leaking out of the intravascular space into tissues. The patient becomes oedematous yet intravascularly dry. This is why you can pour litres of fluid into a septic patient and still find them under-filled — and equally why over-filling drowns their tissues (Session 4).

5 · The vasodilation → maldistribution → hypoperfusion cascade

Now watch the vicious cycle assemble, step by step — this is the engine of septic shock:

  1. Massive nitric-oxide-driven vasodilation. iNOS floods vessels with NO → arterial and venous tone collapse → systemic vascular resistance falls → distributive hypotension. The patient is warm and flushed ("warm shock") despite catastrophic circulatory failure.
  2. Maldistribution of flow. Vasodilation is patchy and uncoordinated. Some capillary beds are over-perfused while others are shunted and starved. Even with a "normal" cardiac output and blood pressure, microvascular flow is heterogeneous — oxygen is delivered to the wrong places.
  3. Capillary leak drops preload. Fluid leaves the vessels → relative hypovolaemia → falling venous return → falling cardiac output.
  4. Microvascular thrombosis. The activated, glycocalyx-stripped endothelium clots. Capillaries plug with microthrombi, physically blocking oxygen delivery even where flow exists.
  5. Tissue hypoperfusion → organ dysfunction. Cells are starved of oxygen → anaerobic metabolism → lactate rises → kidneys, liver, brain, and heart begin to fail. Organ dysfunction is the definition of sepsis, and here is where it is generated.
Vasodilation → maldistribution → hypoperfusion → organ dysfunction. Lactate is the tissues screaming that they cannot breathe.

6 · Immunothrombosis & DIC ⚗️ — when clotting joins the attack

Inflammation and coagulation are not separate systems — they are one system with two names. TNF and IL-6 up-regulate tissue factor; the natural anticoagulants (protein C, antithrombin, tissue-factor-pathway inhibitor) are consumed and down-regulated; fibrinolysis is switched off by a surge in PAI-1. The net result is a strongly pro-thrombotic state.

Widespread microvascular clotting consumes platelets and clotting factors until the patient paradoxically begins to bleed — this is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): clotting and bleeding at once, with a falling platelet count, rising D-dimer, prolonged PT/APTT, and falling fibrinogen. The microthrombi are simultaneously a cause of organ failure and a marker of how dysregulated the host has become.

7 · Cellular energy failure — cytopathic hypoxia 🔋

Even when you restore blood pressure and oxygen delivery, sick cells may still fail to use oxygen. Inflammatory mediators (NO, peroxynitrite, reactive oxygen species) poison the mitochondrial electron transport chain. The cell has oxygen available but cannot make ATP from it — a state called cytopathic (or cytotoxic) hypoxia.

This reframes organ dysfunction as, in part, a protective hibernation: cells that cannot produce energy shut down non-essential functions to survive. It also explains why some organs recover completely once the storm passes — they were stunned, not dead.

💡 Pearl

A normal central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO₂) in a septic patient is not reassuring — it can mean the tissues are too poisoned to extract oxygen (cytopathic hypoxia + microvascular shunting), not that they are well perfused. In sepsis, high venous O₂ can be a sign of dying cells, not healthy ones.

8 · The other half of the storm — immunoparalysis 🥶

The name "cytokine storm" tells only half the story. Almost simultaneously, the body mounts a compensatory anti-inflammatory response (IL-10, TGF-β, soluble cytokine receptors). In many patients — especially those who survive the first days — this over-corrects into a state of profound immunosuppression / immunoparalysis:

  • Apoptosis of lymphocytes → lymphopenia (a marker of poor prognosis).
  • Monocyte "exhaustion" with reduced HLA-DR expression → they can no longer present antigen.
  • Reactivation of latent viruses (CMV, HSV) and vulnerability to secondary and hospital-acquired infections.

This is why late sepsis deaths are often driven by secondary infection in a patient whose immune system has been paralysed — and why the old strategy of simply blocking single cytokines (anti-TNF trials) failed: the host is hyper- and hypo-inflamed at the same time, in different compartments.

FeatureHyper-inflammation (early)Immunoparalysis (later)
Dominant mediatorsTNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6IL-10, TGF-β
Clinical faceFever, vasodilation, shock, DICAnergy, lymphopenia, low monocyte HLA-DR
Main threatOrgan failure, circulatory collapseSecondary/nosocomial infection, viral reactivation
Typical timingHours to first daysDays to weeks
☠️ M&M — "But the antibiotics were working"

A 54-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia was improving on day 3 — fever settled, pressors weaned. The team relaxed. On day 6 he spiked again, grew Candida from his line and reactivated CMV, and died of refractory secondary sepsis. At review, his lymphocyte count had fallen to 0.3 and never recovered — a red flag for immunoparalysis that nobody acted on. Lesson: surviving the first storm is not the same as being safe. The dysregulated host stays dysregulated in both directions; persistent lymphopenia is the tissues telling you the immune system is now the problem.

9 · Putting it together — the wiring diagram of a dysregulated host

Follow the whole chain in one breath: Infection → PAMPs/DAMPs bind PRRs → NF-κB → cytokine storm (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) → endothelial activation + glycocalyx shedding → capillary leak + vasodilation + microvascular thrombosis → maldistributed, hypoperfused, energy-starved tissues → organ dysfunction = sepsis. Overlay a compensatory anti-inflammatory wave that tips into immunoparalysis, and you have the entire disease on one page.

Notice what is not on that diagram: the specific bug. The pathogen is the trigger, but the pathology is the host. That single insight is why source control and antibiotics are necessary but never sufficient — and why everything else this week is about supporting the patient through their own response.

10 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Sepsis = organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response — not the infection itself.
  • PAMPs + DAMPs → PRRs (TLRs) → NF-κB is the ignition; sterile insults use the same wiring.
  • TNF, IL-1, IL-6 drive the storm; the endothelium is where the disease lives.
  • Glycocalyx shedding → capillary leak; iNOS/NO → vasodilation → maldistribution → hypoperfusion.
  • Immunothrombosis/DIC and cytopathic hypoxia complete the organ-failure picture.
  • Immunoparalysis is the deadly second act — watch the lymphocyte count.

Next session: how we take this mechanistic instinct and turn it into a precise, reproducible definition — Sepsis-3, SOFA, and qSOFA at the bedside.

moderatorQs.q: The Sepsis-3 definition deliberately dropped the word 'infection' as sufficient and centred on 'dysregulated host response.' Why does that wording matter clinically?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because it moves the diagnosis — and the urgency — away from the pathogen and onto the patient's physiology. Most infections never become sepsis; what defines sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction generated by the host's own inflammatory, coagulopathic, and vasodilatory response. Clinically this means you cannot 'wait for the culture': the killer is the response already underway, so you resuscitate and treat the organ dysfunction in front of you rather than the microbiology you don't yet have. It also explains why source control plus antibiotics are necessary but never sufficient — they stop the trigger, not the storm.

moderatorQs.q: Anti-TNF and other single-cytokine-blockade trials repeatedly failed in sepsis despite elegant mechanistic rationale. What does that failure teach us about the pathophysiology?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It teaches that sepsis is not a single-cytokine disease you can switch off. The host is simultaneously hyper-inflamed and, in other compartments, profoundly immunosuppressed — a heterogeneous, time-varying state. Blocking TNF in a patient who is already tipping into immunoparalysis can worsen their ability to clear the infection. The lesson is that broad, non-specific suppression of a redundant, feed-forward network (TNF → IL-1 → IL-6, complement, coagulation all cross-activating) rarely helps, and that any future immunomodulation must be patient- and time-specific — which is why prognostic and predictive enrichment is the current research direction.

moderatorQs.q: A patient in septic shock has a normal or even high ScvO₂. Is that reassuring, and what is happening at the cellular level?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It is not reassuring. A high central venous oxygen saturation in sepsis usually means the tissues are failing to extract oxygen, not that they are well supplied. Two mechanisms explain it: microvascular shunting (blood bypasses starved capillary beds because vasodilation is patchy and maldistributed) and cytopathic hypoxia (NO, peroxynitrite and ROS poison the mitochondrial electron transport chain so cells cannot use the oxygen delivered). So oxygen is arriving in the vein unused. A persistently elevated lactate alongside a 'good' ScvO₂ is a red flag that the defect is at the mitochondrion, not just the pump.

audienceQs.q: Why does a septic patient look oedematous and swollen but the team keeps saying they're 'dry' and need fluid?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because the two describe different compartments. Inflammatory mediators shed the endothelial glycocalyx and open the junctions between endothelial cells, so protein-rich fluid leaks out of the vessels into the interstitium — that is the visible oedema. But the fluid that leaked out has left the intravascular space under-filled, so venous return and preload fall — that is being 'dry.' The patient is waterlogged in the tissues and empty in the veins at the same time. This is exactly why fluid resuscitation is a balancing act: too little and you don't fill the tank, too much and you worsen the tissue oedema (covered in Session 4).

audienceQs.q: How does DIC in sepsis manage to cause clotting and bleeding at the same time?
audienceQs.answerHTML: They are two ends of one process. Inflammation up-regulates tissue factor and suppresses the natural anticoagulants (protein C, antithrombin, TFPI) while a surge in PAI-1 shuts down fibrinolysis — so the microvasculature clots widely (immunothrombosis), causing organ ischaemia. That widespread clotting consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. Once consumed, the patient can no longer form clots where they're actually needed, so they bleed — from lines, cannulae, mucosa. Labs show falling platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, high D-dimer and falling fibrinogen. Treat the sepsis; the coagulopathy follows the host response.

audienceQs.q: If the immune system is overreacting, why not just give strong immunosuppression like steroids to everyone?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because the septic host is not simply 'over-active' — it is dysregulated in both directions at once. Alongside the early cytokine storm there is a compensatory anti-inflammatory wave that, in many patients, tips into immunoparalysis (lymphopenia, exhausted monocytes, secondary infections). Blanket immunosuppression can push those patients further into that hole and impair pathogen clearance. Steroids do have a defined, limited role — low-dose hydrocortisone in vasopressor-dependent septic shock — but that is targeted support of the stress response, not global immune shutdown. The take-home: match the intervention to where on the hyper-/hypo-inflammatory spectrum the patient actually is.
